segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: Hi Don – did you get the copy of the article on recyclingfootwear that I emailed you?

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: Yeah – it’s here ... I’ve had a look at it.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: So do you think it’s a good topic for our presentation?

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: Well, before I started reading it, I thought recycling footwear, well, although it’s quite interesting, perhaps there isn’t enough to say about it, cos we put shoes in recycling bins, they go to charity shops and that’s about it.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: ... but there’s much more to it than that.

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: I realise that now and I’m keen to research the topic more.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: That’s great.

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: One of the things I didn’t realise until I read the article was just how many pairs of trainers get recycled!

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: Well, a lot of young people wear them all the time now. They’ve become more popular than ordinary shoes.

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: I know. I guess they are very hard-wearing, but don’t they look a bit casual for school uniform? I don’t think they’re right for that.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: Actually, I think some of them look quite smart on pupils ... better than a scruffy old pair of shoes.

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: So do you keep shoes a long time?

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: Yes. Though I do tend to wear my old pairs for doing dirty jobs like cleaning my bike.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: I must admit, I’ve recycled some perfectly good shoes, that haven’t gone out of fashion and still fit, just because they don’t look great on me any more. That’s awful isn’t it?

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: I think it’s common because there’s so much choice. The article did say that recent sales of footwear have increased enormously.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: That didn’t surprise me.

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: No. But then it said that the amount of recycled footwear has fallen: it’s 6 percent now compared to a previous level of 11 percent. That doesn’t seem to make sense.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: That’s because not everything goes through the recycling process. Some footwear just isn’t good enough to re-sell, for one reason or another, and gets rejected.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: So let’s find some examples in the article of footwear that was rejected for recycling.

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: OK. I think there are some in the interview with the recycling manager. Yeah – here it is.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: Mmm. Let’s start with the ladies’ high-heeled shoes. What did he say about those?

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: He said they were probably expensive – the material was suede and they were beige in colour – it looked like someone had only worn them once, but in a very wet field so the heels were too stained with mud and grass to re-sell them.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: OK ... and the leather ankle boots. What was wrong with them?

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: Apparently, the heels were worn – but that wasn’t the problem. One of the shoes was a much lighter shade than the other one – it had obviously been left in the sun. I suppose even second-hand shoes should look the same!

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: Sure. Then there were the red baby shoes.

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: Oh yes – we’re told to tie shoes together when we put them in a recycling bin, but people often don’t bother.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: You’d think it would have been easy to find the other, but it wasn’t. That was a shame because they were obviously new.

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: The trainers were interesting. He said they looked like they’d been worn by a marathon runner.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: Yeah – weren’t they split?

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: Not exactly. One of the soles was so worn under the foot that you could put your finger through it.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: Well, we could certainly use some of those examples in our presentation to explain why 90 percent of shoes that people take to recycling centres or bins get thrown into landfill.

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: Mmm. What did you think about the project his team set up to avoid this by making new shoes out of the good parts of old shoes?

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: It sounded like a good idea. They get so many shoes, they should be able to match parts. I wasn’t surprised that it failed, though. I mean who wants to buy second-hand shoes really? Think of all the germs you could catch!

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: Well, people didn’t refuse them for that reason, did they? It was because the pairs of shoes weren’t identical.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: They still managed to ship them overseas, though.

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: That’s another area we need to discuss.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: You know I used to consider this topic just from my own perspective, by thinking about my own recycling behaviour without looking at the bigger picture. So much happens once shoes leave the recycling area.

segments.speaker: DON
segments.en: It’s not as simple as you first think, and we can show that by taking a very different approach to it.

segments.speaker: BELLA
segments.en: Absolutely. So let’s discuss ...
